definition.text: A study of the likely environmental effects of a project, plan or policy, done before anyone decides whether to go ahead with it.

facts.text: Its aim is to make sure that the people deciding on a project take its environmental effects into account.
An EIA does not demand a set environmental outcome; it requires decision-makers to weigh environmental values and justify their choice using studies and public comments.
EIAs began in the 1960s amid growing environmental awareness, and in the United States gained formal status with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
More than 180 countries use environmental impact assessments, making them a widely used tool of international environmental governance.
At the end of a project an audit can compare actual impacts with predicted ones, to check the predictions and how well mitigation worked.
Few national EIA laws explicitly require assessing a project's contribution to climate change.
Biodiversity offsetting is often applied through EIA processes, guided by the mitigation hierarchy.

definition.text: In United States law, a document required under the National Environmental Policy Act for federal actions that significantly affect the quality of the human environment.

facts.text: An EIS describes the good and bad environmental effects of a proposed action and usually lists alternative actions that could be chosen instead.
A shorter environmental assessment is prepared first to decide whether a full EIS is needed; it ends in either a Finding of No Significant Impact or an EIS.
The adequacy of an EIS can be challenged in federal court, and major projects have been blocked because an agency failed to prepare an acceptable one.

title: Criticisms of environmental impact assessment

definition.text: Objections that environmental impact assessments are too narrow in scope, handle uncertainty poorly, have little influence on decisions and can delay projects.

facts.text: In practice almost all EIAs address only direct, immediate on-site effects, although indirect effects of development can be much larger.
Because EIA aids decisions rather than making them, some argue its influence on decisions is limited.
Researchers argue that uncertainties get too little systematic attention in environmental studies.
EIAs can delay environmentally friendly projects and raise their costs.

contested_note: Critics and practitioners disagree about how much influence EIAs have on decisions and how wide their scope should be.

definition.text: Assessing the environmental effects of a project that cross national borders, such as pollution reaching another country.

facts.text: The Espoo Convention of the UN Economic Commission for Europe provides an international legal framework for transboundary EIA.
With no world legislature, international treaties develop in parallel and are hard to enforce, which has led to duplications and failures.
International advisory opinions in 2024 and 2025 confirmed that EIAs must consider harm beyond national borders, including to the global climate system.

title: Porter hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that strict environmental regulation can push firms to become more efficient and innovative, improving their competitiveness.

facts.text: Economist Michael Porter proposed it in 1991, and with Claas van der Linde set it out in detail in a 1995 article.
Regulation is said to trigger cleaner technologies (the innovation effect) whose cost savings more than cover compliance and innovation costs.
Firms in early-regulating countries may gain a first-mover advantage through learning effects or patents.
Studies support the 'weak' version, that stricter regulation stimulates innovation, but evidence is mixed for the 'strong' version, that it boosts business performance.
A study of OECD countries found no permanent effect of tighter environmental policy on productivity, whatever the type of regulation.
The idea is often cited in support of green growth.

contested_note: Evidence is mixed on whether stricter regulation actually improves business performance.

definition.text: A legal limit on how much of a given air pollutant a particular source may release over a set period.

facts.text: Emission standards are usually designed to achieve air quality standards and protect human life.
Many target cars and other vehicles; others cover industry, power plants and small equipment such as lawn mowers and diesel generators.
The first car emission standards were enacted in the United States in 1963, mainly in response to smog in Los Angeles; Japan followed three years later.
Different regions and countries set different vehicle standards.
Higher emission standards are one way to make sure efficiency gains actually cut fuel use, alongside green taxes and cap and trade.

definition.text: A limit on emissions above which a different type of emission-control technology may be needed.

facts.text: Such standards have limited conventional pollutants such as nitrogen and sulphur oxides and may also be used for carbon dioxide.
In the US the limit is given in pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt-hour; elsewhere in kilograms per megawatt-hour.

definition.text: The European Union's set of emission limits that all new road vehicles must meet, graded in stages such as Euro 4, Euro 5 and Euro 6.

facts.text: They cover all road vehicles, trains, barges and non-road machinery such as tractors, but not seagoing ships or aircraft.
EU Regulation No 443/2009 set an average CO2 target for new cars of 130 grams per kilometre, tightened to 95 grams per kilometre from 2021.
Many other countries adopt the Euro stages, for example all new vehicles in ECOWAS must meet Euro 4 since 2021.

title: Environmental law

definition.text: The body of treaties, statutes, regulations and policies meant to protect the natural environment and manage how human activity affects ecosystems and natural resources.

facts.text: It covers pollution control, resource conservation, biodiversity protection, climate change mitigation and sustainable development.
Under the old common law the main protection was the law of nuisance, which allowed only private lawsuits when land was harmed and proved inadequate for threats to shared resources.
London's Great Smog of 1952 led to the Clean Air Act 1956, which set emission limits for households and businesses enforced by an inspectorate.
Pollution-control laws cover air quality, water quality, waste management, contaminant cleanup and chemical safety; resource laws cover water, minerals, forests, wildlife and fish and game.
Debates continue over the necessity, fairness and cost of environmental regulation, and over whether regulations or market solutions better achieve agreed goals.
Regulated industries commonly argue against regulation on grounds of cost, while many environmental groups argue current rules are too weak.
Smaller firms can bear disproportionately large costs from environmental regulation, which can become a barrier to entry for new firms.

contested_note: The necessity, fairness and cost of environmental regulation, and regulation versus market solutions, remain debated.

definition.text: A set of guiding ideas, not universally accepted, that run through environmental law, such as sustainable development, equity, prevention, precaution and polluter pays.

facts.text: Equity includes intergenerational equity, the right of future generations to a fair share of the common inheritance, and intragenerational equity among people alive today.
Transboundary responsibility is an obligation to protect one's own environment and prevent damage to neighbouring ones, which can limit a sovereign state's rights.
Prevention is an overarching aim served by prior assessment of harm, licensing, emission limits and best available techniques.
The Rio Declaration's precautionary principle says lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective measures against serious or irreversible damage.
The polluter pays principle holds that environmental costs of economic activity, including preventing harm, should be borne by those causing them rather than by society at large.
Public participation and transparency appear in environmental impact assessment, laws on access to environmental data, and administrative procedure.

definition.text: The part of international law dealing with global and regional environmental problems, made up of treaties, customary rules and the decisions of international courts.

facts.text: Most international environmental agreements are multilateral treaties, often filled out later by protocols that can add new scientific knowledge.
Protocols let countries agree on a framework that would be too contentious if every detail had to be settled first; the Kyoto Protocol is the best-known example.
Customary rules include the duty to warn other states promptly of environmental dangers they face.
A major challenge in international decisions is setting adequate compensation for environmental damage.

definition.text: Laws governing the removal of pollution from soil, sediment, surface water or groundwater after contamination has happened.

facts.text: Unlike pollution-control laws, cleanup laws respond after the fact, so they must define both the needed response and who must carry it out or pay for it.
Their rules may cover emergency response, liability allocation, site assessment, remedial action, monitoring after cleanup and site reuse.

definition.text: Laws that govern the release of air pollutants into the atmosphere, mostly to protect human health.

facts.text: Regulators identify and classify pollutants, set limits on acceptable emissions and prescribe control technologies.
The US Clean Air Act names six 'criteria' pollutants for nationwide regulation: ozone, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and lead.
Some air laws address wider ecological problems, such as ozone-depleting chemicals or emissions trading for acid rain and climate change.

definition.text: A systematic process for making sure environmental, and sometimes wider sustainability, effects are considered when policies, plans and programmes are made.

facts.text: It grew from a weakness of project-level EIA: many damaging choices are made earlier at a strategic level, for example new infrastructure that generates more travel.
An SEA usually comes before the related project EIAs, so its findings cascade down the tiers of decision-making and reduce later work.
Under the EU directive its phases are screening, scoping, a baseline of the environment, estimating likely impacts, influencing the decision and monitoring afterwards.
The EU SEA Directive 2001/42/EC made SEA legally required for many regional, local, development, waste and transport plans.
The UNECE Protocol on Strategic Environmental Assessment came into force in July 2010 and, unlike the EU directive, can be applied to policies and legislation.
Donors use SEA in development co-operation to make sure aid delivered through strategic-level interventions considers the environment.

definition.text: The technology or techniques that regulators approve as the standard for meeting a process's output limits, such as for pollution control.

facts.text: It is a moving target, since changing values and advancing techniques shift what counts as 'best available'.
Read literally it would demand the best technology regardless of cost, but in practice costs are also taken into account.
The older UK idea of 'best practicable means' appeared in the Salmon Fishery Act 1861; the EEC introduced 'best available techniques not entailing excessive costs' in 1984.
Under the EU Industrial Emissions Directive, BAT conclusions are the reference for permit conditions of large industrial installations, without prescribing any particular technology.
Under the US Clean Water Act, EPA picks a model technology, sets a numeric discharge limit based on it, and lets each facility meet that limit with any technology.
BAT standards are a classic example of command-and-control regulation, in contrast to emissions trading.

title: Command and control regulation

definition.text: Direct regulation by law that states what an industry or activity may and may not do, backed by penalties for breaking the rules.

facts.text: The 'command' is a standard or target set by a government authority; the 'control' is the sanction, such as prosecution, for not complying.
It differs from using economic incentives such as taxes and subsidies to encourage compliance.
In environmental policy it relies on three main kinds of standards: ambient standards, emission standards and technology standards, usually used in combination.
It dominated environmental policy in industrial nations in the 1970s, when the focus was on remedying problems rather than broad prevention.
It works fairly well for point sources but struggles with diffuse sources: ten big power stations are easy to regulate, millions of motorists are not.
Uniform sanctions can make small businesses feel the burden of regulation more than large companies.
Some commentators prefer the term 'direct regulatory instrument' because 'command and control' carries negative connotations.

distinct_from: Command and control versus economic incentives
Command and control and global environmental problems

title: Command and control versus economic incentives

definition.text: The long-running argument over whether direct rules or price-based tools such as taxes and tradable permits protect the environment at lower cost.

facts.text: Critics call command and control inefficient; a summary of 10 studies found significant cost differences between it and least-cost alternatives.
A carbon tax, unlike classic command and control, lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution instead of limiting each polluter.
Defenders note that incentive schemes need monitoring and administration too, so their total costs can sometimes be higher.
Incentive schemes often need complex rules, inspection and enforcement that make them resemble command and control.
Supporters of direct rules say fixed legal standards let regulators respond quickly to violations and give clarity to those regulated.
Enthusiasm for economic incentives has grown since the 1970s, partly from disenchantment with command and control.

contested_note: Economists often favour incentives as cheaper, while others argue direct regulation can be less costly once monitoring and administration are counted.
distinct_from: Command and control and global environmental problems

title: Types of command-and-control standards

definition.text: The kinds of standards direct regulation uses: general environmental standards, target standards about the receiving environment, and performance standards on releases.

facts.text: Target standards split into ambient standards, which set goals for regulators, and receptor standards, maximum levels the regulated must not exceed.
Performance standards determine what releases of a pollutant are acceptable.
Which standard is used depends on the nature of the problem and the administrative capacity of the government.

distinct_from: Command and control versus economic incentives
Command and control and global environmental problems

title: Command and control and global environmental problems

definition.text: The question of how well direct regulation, built for national governments, can work for problems that cross borders, such as ozone depletion and climate change.

facts.text: The 1987 Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting chlorofluorocarbons is often cited as an international command-and-control success, though some see it as a special case.
Climate change is often used to show its failings: the problem is complex, uncertain and needs more proactive action than traditional models deliver.
Because it relies on prohibitions enforced by sanctions, scaling it up to the international level is problematic.
A blend of approaches and actors, including environmental NGOs, may be the best answer.

contested_note: Commentators disagree whether the Montreal Protocol shows command and control can work globally or is a special case.
distinct_from: Command and control versus economic incentives

definition.text: Taxes proposed or imposed to raise money for dealing with global warming, or to discourage the activities that cause it.

facts.text: The British economist Arthur Pigou advocated corrective taxes for pollution in the early 20th century, which is why they are called Pigovian taxes.
Using a Pigovian tax against global warming was proposed as far back as 1992 by economist Martin Feldstein.
A San Francisco Bay Area fee on carbon dioxide emissions was meant to pay for monitoring greenhouse gases rather than to deter emissions.

title: Meat tax

definition.text: A tax on meat or other animal products meant to cover the health and environmental costs of using animals for food.

facts.text: Livestock contributes significantly to global warming and harms global nitrogen cycles and biodiversity.
Researchers and groups such as Chatham House have called for taxes on red meat or high-emission foods, citing climate and health benefits.
Opponents call it regressive and authoritarian or doubt its health and economic claims.
In June 2024 Denmark announced a tax on livestock carbon dioxide emissions from 2030, the first country to do so.

contested_note: Supporters cite climate and health gains; opponents call the tax regressive and doubt its claims.

title: Clean Air Act (United States)

definition.text: The main United States federal law for preventing and reducing air pollution, first passed in 1963 and greatly expanded by later amendments.

facts.text: The 1970 amendments created national ambient air quality standards, performance standards for new sources and standards for hazardous air pollutants, and strengthened federal enforcement.
States write implementation plans to meet the Act's requirements and EPA reviews and approves them, a cooperative model reflecting the need for local knowledge.
The 1990 amendments created the Acid Rain Program, the first US cap-and-trade programme, to cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from power plants.
EPA's removal of lead from US gasoline from 1971 has been called one of the great public health achievements of the 20th century.
A 2022 review found overwhelming causal evidence that the Act improved air quality.
A 2011 EPA study projected that by 2020 the 1990 amendments would cost about $60 billion a year while yielding about $2 trillion a year in health benefits.
EPA began regulating greenhouse gases after the 2007 Supreme Court ruling in Massachusetts v. EPA and its later endangerment finding.
Ethnic-minority people in the US are 1.5 times more likely than majority people to live in areas burdened by air pollution.

notes: US statute kept as one entry: navbox page with 27 in-scope inlinks and a standard case of command-and-control and cost-benefit evidence.

definition.text: United States limits on the concentration in outdoor air of six pollutants that cause smog, acid rain and other health hazards.

facts.text: The six 'criteria' pollutants are ozone, particulate matter, lead, carbon monoxide, sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides.
Primary standards protect health; secondary standards protect other public welfare, such as agricultural values.
Areas that miss the standards are 'nonattainment areas' and must plan for 'reasonable further progress'.
A 2025 study found the standards produced more than a trillion dollars in welfare gains since 1997.

title: Clean Water Act

definition.text: The main United States federal law controlling pollution of surface waters, adopted as the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972.

facts.text: It created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System: point sources such as factories and sewage plants may not discharge into surface waters without a permit.
Farm stormwater and irrigation return flows were exempted as nonpoint sources; Congress instead funded research and assistance to improve farm runoff practices.
The 1972 Act paid for municipal sewage treatment plants through grants, with federal funds covering 75% of project costs.
Any citizen may sue someone who violates a discharge permit, after giving 60 days' notice.
Its 1983 'fishable and swimmable' goal has not been met: more than half of stream and river miles and about 70 percent of lakes still violate water quality standards.
Analysts credit it with controlling point sources but say it has not worked for nonpoint sources.
Section 404 of the Act is the legal basis for wetland mitigation banking in the United States.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether its benefits justify its costs and how much it reduced water pollution.
notes: US statute kept as one entry: 36 in-scope inlinks and the basis of US wetland banking and offsets.

definition.text: Two layers of discharge limits under the Clean Water Act: a national floor based on what control technology can achieve, topped up by stricter limits where a water body stays polluted.

facts.text: Technology-based standards are set for whole categories of dischargers from the performance of control technologies, regardless of the receiving water.
Congress meant them to create a 'level playing field' with a basic national standard for every facility in a category.
Water quality standards have four parts: designated uses, water quality criteria, an antidegradation policy and general policies.

title: Clean Water Act section 404 permits
article: Clean Water Act#Dredge and fill permits

definition.text: Permits required under the US Clean Water Act before dredged or fill material may be placed in streams, wetlands and other regulated waters.

facts.text: They are issued by the US Army Corps of Engineers and are key to protecting wetlands that developers would otherwise fill.
Biodiversity banking grew out of US wetland mitigation banking and the 'no net loss' policies tied to the Act in the 1970s.
Its application to farming caused controversy, and the 1977 amendments added six exemptions for activities such as normal farming.

title: Corporate average fuel economy

definition.text: United States rules, first enacted in 1975 after the 1973-74 oil embargo, requiring the cars and light trucks each maker sells to meet an average fuel economy.

facts.text: CAFE does not reward buyers or change fuel prices; it works indirectly by penalising automakers that build inefficient vehicles.
A 2002 National Academy of Sciences report found fuel use would have been about 14 percent higher without CAFE, but lighter vehicles may have caused 1,300 to 2,600 extra deaths in 1993.
Since 2008 targets depend on a vehicle's 'footprint' (wheelbase times track width), so makers of larger vehicles face lower targets.
Certifying minivans and later SUVs as trucks let makers meet the less strict truck standard, contributing to their rise.
Better fuel efficiency leads people to drive more: a 10% efficiency gain raises travel distance by an average of 1-2%.
Since 2007 makers can trade fuel-economy credits between vehicle categories and sell them to others.
Critics argue the fines were too small to matter; in 2025 they were eliminated, effectively mooting the standards.

contested_note: The safety effects, costs and real fuel savings of CAFE are actively debated.
notes: US programme kept as the course's worked example of a fuel-economy performance standard.

title: Endangered Species Act of 1973

definition.text: The main United States law for protecting imperilled species, signed in 1973 to stop extinctions caused by economic growth that ignored conservation.

facts.text: Its two aims are to prevent extinction and to recover species until the law's protection is no longer needed.
Agencies list species as 'endangered' or the lesser 'threatened'; Section 9 bans 'take', meaning to harass, harm or hunt them.
Since 1982, listing decisions must be made solely on biological and trade information, without weighing economic effects.
Habitat loss is the main threat to most imperilled species, so the Act lets agencies designate 'critical habitat' zones.
By August 2023, 1,780 species had been listed; 99% were still alive but only 64 had recovered enough to be removed from the list.
The American alligator, listed in 1967, was delisted as fully recovered twenty years later.
It underpins US conservation banking, which offsets harm to species protected under the Act.

contested_note: It is described as one of the most powerful and controversial US environmental laws, chiefly over its economic costs.
distinct_from: Perverse incentives of endangered species protection
notes: US statute kept as one entry: 28 in-scope inlinks; basis of US conservation banking.

title: Perverse incentives of endangered species protection
article: Endangered Species Act of 1973#Economic consequences and perverse incentives

definition.text: The problem that strict species-protection rules can make an endangered species a financial burden for landowners, tempting them to destroy habitat before the species arrives.

facts.text: Because species could be listed without considering economic costs, the Act soon became controversial; landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays.
A 1995 study of about 1,000 private forest plots found owners more likely to harvest pines as they matured enough to attract endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers.
The western saying 'shoot, shovel, and shut up' sums up the extreme form of this response.
Economists suggest compensating property owners for protecting species, so a listed species is not seen as a potential financial loss.
Agreements between landowners and the agency helped the woodpecker be downlisted from endangered to threatened by 2024.

contested_note: Many hold that protections curtail economic activity and create perverse incentives, while others defend the Act's species-first approach.

definition.text: A rule, regulation or practice, usually set by government, that says how the environment must be treated and kept, such as a pollution limit or a permit requirement.

facts.text: Standards can ban specific activities, fix how often and how monitoring is done, or require permits to use land or water.
They rest on scientific opinion from several fields, public views and social context, so setting them is complex.
Their development has been shaped by two competing views: ecocentrism, which gives nature intrinsic value, and anthropocentrism, which values it only for human survival.
European legislation sets precise pollutant concentrations as well as target concentrations to be reached by given dates.
US EPA technology standards set minimum performance levels rather than requiring specific technologies, often based on the industry's top performers.
The ISO 14001 environmental management standard is held by about 363,000 companies and organisations worldwide.

title: Voluntary corporate environmental standards

definition.text: Environmental standards that companies adopt for themselves, beyond what the law requires, usually to satisfy customers, governments and industry partners.

facts.text: Government is the strongest influence on companies' standards, followed by customers and then industry networks with codes of conduct.
Companies are often said to focus on how their commitments look in advertising rather than on real implementation.
Whether self-imposed environmental standards are effective is controversial.

contested_note: It is disputed whether companies' self-commitment standards actually change environmental outcomes.

title: Harrington paradox

definition.text: The puzzle that firms mostly obey environmental rules even though inspections are rare, violators are seldom punished and expected fines are small next to compliance costs.

facts.text: Winston Harrington first described it in a 1988 paper based on US enforcement data from the late 1970s and early 1980s.
It contradicts Gary Becker's rational-crime theory, under which a profit-maximising firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying.
Harrington's own explanation is targeted enforcement: regulators inspect more often the firms more likely to be violating, instead of at random.
Other explanations include leniency for firms that self-report violations, and firms' altruism or concern for their self-image.
Empirical evidence is rare: in Norway most firms had minor deviations, while major violations faced strict punishment, consistent with Becker's theory.

prerequisites: Economics of crime and optimal enforcement
contested_note: Researchers question whether the paradox really exists, since evidence is scarce and major violations do face heavy penalties.

title: Low-carbon fuel standard

definition.text: A tradable-credit rule that requires the average carbon intensity of a region's transport fuels to fall below that of petrol and diesel.

facts.text: It counts emissions over the fuel's whole life cycle, 'well to wheels', not just from the tailpipe.
California enacted the first one in 2007, aiming for at least a 10 percent cut in transport fuel carbon intensity by 2020.
Whether to count emissions from indirect land-use change caused by biofuels was fiercely debated by scientists and the biofuel industry.
Canada requires liquid fossil fuel suppliers to cut carbon intensity to 15% below 2016 levels by 2030.

related: Indirect land use change impacts of biofuels
contested_note: Scientists disagreed on whether indirect land-use emissions from biofuels could be estimated well enough to include.

definition.text: An area, usually in a city, where polluting vehicles are barred or charged for entering, to improve air quality.

facts.text: Many zones do not physically block entry but fine non-compliant vehicles unless a daily charge has been paid, often checked by number-plate cameras.
They work: diesel particulates fall in most zones and health improves, often because people replace polluting vehicles with cleaner ones.
People who need a car but cannot afford a cleaner one are hit hardest, so some cities enforce zones only where public transport exists or subsidise alternatives.
As of 2019 there were about 250 low-emission zones helping meet EU health-based air quality limits; London's, from 2008, was the world's largest.

title: Minimum energy performance standard

definition.text: A mandatory specification that caps how much energy an appliance or other device may use to do a given task.

facts.text: It usually requires a set test procedure, and may include non-energy requirements so that performance and user satisfaction do not suffer.
A refrigerator, for example, must hold set temperatures while using at most a specified amount of electricity, depending on its size and features.
California began appliance efficiency rules in 1978, and they became US national standards in 1988.
Standards are often paired with energy rating labels that help consumers choose products using less energy.

notes: The page's 'Left field' section (e.g. S:9239228d43cf, S:2e7ae5d7f0e5) is vandalised nonsense; none of it is cited.

title: National Environmental Policy Act

definition.text: The 1969 United States law, in force from 1970, that requires federal agencies to weigh environmental effects before acting and created the Council on Environmental Quality.

facts.text: It grew out of 1960s environmental concern, fed by Silent Spring, the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill and protests against highway building.
Agencies follow three levels of review: a categorical exclusion, an environmental assessment ending in a finding of no significant impact, or a full environmental impact statement.
The history of EIA in other countries, such as Australia, is linked to NEPA's requirement for environmental impact statements.
A federal study of 2013-2018 found a full NEPA review took an average of 4.5 years.
With no enforcement power at the Council, violations go through the courts; the usual remedy is ordering the review to be redone.
Evidence on its costs and benefits is limited: reviews have grown longer, while case studies suggest it curbed some of the worst abuses.
NEPA is the law most used in US climate change litigation, with 322 cases filed.

contested_note: Defenders see it as a key safeguard, while critics blame it for long delays; changes under successive administrations reflect this dispute.
notes: US statute kept as one entry: the model for environmental impact assessment worldwide; 13 in-scope inlinks.

title: Natura 2000

definition.text: The European Union's network of protected nature areas on land and at sea, designated under the Birds and Habitats Directives.

facts.text: It joins Special Protection Areas for birds under the 1979 Birds Directive with Special Areas of Conservation under the 1992 Habitats Directive.
In 2022 it covered more than 18% of the EU's land area and more than 7% of its marine area.
Sites are not strictly closed to people: many are farmed, forested or even urban.
Designation is nearly complete, but management and enforcement lag and many sites lack management plans.
Its benefits are estimated at €200-300 billion a year.
Developers, farmers and politicians criticise it as a brake on development, and its habitats assessment triggered the Dutch nitrogen crisis.

contested_note: Developers and farmers see it as blocking development; legal scholars question whether its habitats test fits climate and ecosystem-service goals.

definition.text: Pollution of air, water, heat, noise or light that comes from a single identifiable source, such as a factory outlet or smokestack.

facts.text: It is called a point source because in models it can be treated as a single mathematical point.
Examples include factories, power plants, sewage treatment plants and some farms such as concentrated animal feeding operations.
It contrasts with nonpoint sources, diffuse pollution from wide areas such as urban and farm runoff.
Direct regulation works relatively well for point sources but struggles with diffuse, nonpoint pollution.
Carbon capture and storage captures carbon dioxide from large point sources such as cement factories.

definition.text: The laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measurement of pollution levels.

facts.text: Locally, regulation is usually overseen by environmental agencies or the public health system.
The modern regulatory system began with US rules on industrial and mining air and water pollution in the 1960s and 1970s.
Because many pollutants cross borders, UN treaties regulate them, such as the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting chemicals in 1987.
Polluters have historically lobbied governments of poorer countries to keep regulation lax.

title: Pollution prevention
article: Regulation and monitoring of pollution#Pollution prevention

definition.text: A strategy of cutting the amount of waste created in the first place, rather than treating it after release, especially by industry, farms and consumers.

facts.text: Many large corporations see it as a way to make production more efficient and profitable through less waste and better technology.
In the US it was written into law through the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 and the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments.

title: Regulatory economics

definition.text: The study and use of government rules to achieve economic aims, such as correcting market failures and protecting the environment.

facts.text: Regulation is law imposed by government on people and private firms to change economic behaviour; some industries instead regulate themselves.
Government agencies are always at risk of regulatory capture by the industries they regulate.
Principal-agent theory treats the government as principal and the regulated operator as agent, to deal with the operator knowing more than the regulator.
Supporters argue regulation guards against monopoly, instability and environmental harm, drawing on thinkers such as Karl Polanyi.
Economists such as Milton Friedman, George Stigler and Friedrich Hayek argue for limiting government's role in markets.
Regulatory intervention can counter a market failure, so some economists think some regulation beats an unregulated market.

contested_note: Economists disagree sharply on whether regulation generally improves or worsens market outcomes.
distinct_from: Positive and normative theories of regulation

title: Positive and normative theories of regulation

definition.text: Two families of theory: positive theories explain why regulation happens, normative theories say how regulators should act.

facts.text: Positive theories say regulation arises to overcome information gaps, protect customers from market power, protect operators from rivals or from government opportunism.
Normative theories say regulators should reduce information costs, set efficient prices and run independent, transparent and predictable processes.

definition.text: A rule requiring electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources such as wind, solar, biomass and geothermal.

facts.text: Certified renewable generators earn certificates for each unit of electricity, sell them to suppliers, who hand them to the regulator to prove compliance.
Supporters say relying on the market brings competition and innovation that deliver renewable energy at the lowest cost.
RPS-type schemes exist in the UK, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Chile and in 29 of 50 US states.
A US national laboratory credits state standards with 60% of the rise in US renewable electricity since 2000, though their share of new builds is falling.
Like subsidies, renewable portfolio standards create protected markets for renewable energy, an alternative to feed-in tariffs.

title: Superfund

definition.text: The common name for the 1980 US law (CERCLA) and its trust fund that pay for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites and make polluters liable for the costs.

facts.text: Congress passed it in 1980 in response to hazardous waste disasters such as Love Canal in New York.
Because responsible parties were hard to find, it set up a fund financed by taxes on certain industries plus a broad liability framework.
Liability is generally joint and several: each potentially responsible party can be held liable for the whole cleanup cost, then seek contributions from others.
Historically about 70 percent of Superfund cleanups have been paid for by potentially responsible parties.
Until the mid-1990s an excise tax on the petroleum and chemical industries funded it, reflecting polluter pays; after it lapsed, taxpayers bore most costs until a chemical tax returned in 2021.
Sites are scored from 0 to 100 by a Hazard Ranking System; a score of 28.5 puts a site on the National Priorities List for long-term cleanup.
Its strict, no-fault liability has been blamed for creating brownfields, as investors avoid contaminated land for greenfield sites.
Minority and low-income communities have had less chance of getting nearby sites listed and cleaned up than richer areas.

notes: US programme kept as the course's main example of liability-based cleanup and polluter-pays funding; 12 in-scope inlinks.

title: Zoning

definition.text: A way for a local government to divide land into zones, each with its own rules on what may be built and how the land may be used.

facts.text: Zones may allow a single use such as housing or industry, mix compatible uses, or, in form-based zoning, govern building size and shape whatever the use.
Single-use zoning separates uses thought incompatible; in practice it also protects existing uses and a community's character.
Overlay zones add rules for a particular concern such as wetlands or a natural hazard without rewriting the whole code.
Environmental activists argue that separating everyday uses forces car ownership and increases traffic.
Some economists say zoning reduces efficiency and raises housing costs; one 2017 study estimated large GDP gains from partial deregulation.
Zoning regulations and land-use measures are key institutional tools for climate change adaptation and flood management in cities.

contested_note: Critics argue zoning raises housing costs, inequality and car dependence, while supporters see it as essential to separate harmful uses.

definition.text: Flexible zoning approaches that judge projects by their effects or let developers build more in return for public benefits such as open space.

facts.text: Performance zoning, first advocated by Lane Kendig in 1973, may let developers earn points for limiting environmental impacts or adding public amenities.
US cities most often use incentive zoning to win mixed use, open space conservation, walkability, affordable housing and parks.
Cluster zoning lets homes sit closer together so more land is kept as open space.

title: Performance and technology standards

definition.text: The two main forms of direct pollution rules: a performance standard sets a numerical emission limit for each polluter, while a technology standard dictates the equipment it must use.

facts.text: A performance standard is typically a numeric limit measured at the discharge point, and the facility may meet it with any technology it chooses.
Regulators often base a performance standard on a model technology, as US EPA does for industrial wastewater.
Letting firms choose how to meet the limit makes performance standards slightly more efficient than technology standards.
Both are less cost-effective than cap and trade, because the burden of cutting emissions cannot shift to firms that can cut more cheaply.
Examples include the US New Source Performance Standards for new industrial facilities and EU CO2 performance standards for new cars.
Technology standards are easy to monitor and enforce, since a regulator can check a car's design for a catalytic converter, which is why lawmakers often control tools rather than behavior.
They give no incentive to change other behavior, such as miles driven, and can backfire: early water-efficient toilets led people to flush repeatedly.
The Cabezas text calls technology standards the worst tool for promoting innovation, because firms are forbidden to use any other technology, even a cheaper one.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own (phrase dossier); also overlaps 'Types of command-and-control standards' (Command and control regulation#Application).

title: Environmental enforcement and compliance

definition.text: The work of checking whether polluters and other regulated parties follow environmental rules, and of penalising those who do not.

facts.text: Under the US Clean Air Act, EPA monitors compliance, seeks penalties and compels violators to comply, but cases usually settle with penalties well below the legal maximum.
The Acid Rain Program required continuous emissions monitoring to ensure compliance and give credibility to allowance trading.
In China strict central rules are monitored and enforced mostly by local governments more interested in economic growth.
International environmental agreements are criticised for lacking monitoring and enforcement.

related: Economics of crime and optimal enforcement
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; sentences are scattered across pages.

title: Economics of crime and optimal enforcement

definition.text: Gary Becker's approach of treating rule-breaking as a rational choice: a profit-maximising firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying.

facts.text: Becker applied economic reasoning to crime and other non-market behaviour, assuming people act rationally.
His model assumes random inspection, whereas real regulators target firms more likely to be violating.
The same logic predicts illicit markets wherever the expected net return from evasion exceeds what is available legally.

notes: Phrase concept with thin support: most phrase-dossier hits are about Becker's other work; only the Harrington paradox page states the model.

title: Environmental liability

definition.text: The legal responsibility of a polluter to pay for preventing and repairing the environmental damage it causes.

facts.text: The EU's 2004 Environmental Liability Directive, on preventing and remedying environmental damage, is based on the polluter pays principle.
Under US Superfund, liability is generally joint and several among responsible parties, and sellers of land cannot pass liability for past contamination to unknowing buyers.
Environmental liability insurance covers injury, property damage and cleanup costs from the release of pollutants.
Before modern statutes, the common law of nuisance allowed only private suits when land was harmed.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Natural resource damage assessment

definition.text: A legal process in which public trustees measure the harm done to natural resources by pollution, so the polluter can be made to pay for restoring them.

facts.text: Superfund authorises federal, state or tribal natural resource trustees to carry out such assessments.
After the Deepwater Horizon spill, federal agencies and five Gulf states formed a trustee council; its assessment found extensive ecological injuries across the Gulf of Mexico.
A 2016 settlement included up to $8.8 billion for natural resource damage assessment and restoration.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Biofuel

definition.text: A fuel made over a short time span from biomass, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form fossil fuels.

facts.text: Biofuel can come from plants or from agricultural, domestic or industrial bio waste, and is mostly used for transport but also for heating and electricity.

Biofuels are regarded as a renewable energy source, yet they face criticism over the food-versus-fuel debate, varied sustainability assessments, and deforestation and biodiversity loss from production.
Global production was 81 Mtoe in 2017, about 3% a year above 2010. The US led with 37 Mtoe, then Brazil and South America at 23 Mtoe and Europe at 12 Mtoe.

Emissions are not inherently carbon-neutral: they depend on feedstock, processing, transport and land-use change, and range from -127.1 gCO2eq per MJ with carbon capture to above 95 gCO2eq per MJ where land-use change is large.
EU and UK policies require biofuels to deliver at least 65% greenhouse gas savings against fossil fuels (70% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin).
The International Resource Panel concluded that biofuels differ in their effects on climate, energy security and ecosystems, so effects should be assessed over the whole life cycle.

related: Indirect land use change from biofuels

definition.text: Alcohol, most commonly ethanol, made by fermenting sugars or starches (or harder, cellulose) with microorganisms and enzymes for use as fuel.

facts.text: Ethanol is the most common biofuel worldwide, especially in Brazil.
The IEA estimated that ethanol production took 20% of sugar supplies and 13% of corn supplies in 2021.
Up to 40% of US corn is turned into ethanol, and worldwide about 10% of all grain is made into biofuel.

definition.text: A liquid fuel made from oils or fats by transesterification, similar in composition to fossil diesel and made mostly of fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters.

facts.text: Biodiesel is the most common biofuel in Europe.
Feedstocks include animal fats, vegetable oils, soy, rapeseed, jatropha, palm oil and algae.
The IEA estimated biodiesel production used 17% of global vegetable oil supplies in 2021.
The European Commission approved a measure to phase out palm oil-based biofuels by 2030, because unsustainable palm oil farming has caused deforestation and pollution.

definition.text: A biofuel for aircraft, also called bio-jet fuel or sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

facts.text: The International Air Transport Association regards it as a key way to cut aviation's environmental impact.
As a drop-in replacement it needs no major aircraft engine changes, so it can decarbonize hard-to-abate medium and long-haul flights.

definition.text: A gas mixture of mainly methane and carbon dioxide, produced by microorganisms digesting organic material without oxygen.

facts.text: It can come from biodegradable waste or from energy crops fed into anaerobic digesters to raise gas yields.
A biodigester can process manure, food waste, agricultural residues, fats, oils and wastewater solids, leaving digestate that can serve as fertilizer or soil amendment.

title: Food vs fuel debate

definition.text: The dispute over whether growing crops for biofuel competes with food production.

facts.text: Biofuel production can compete with food crops; the text says a 50% cut in grain used for biofuels in the US and Europe would replace all of Ukraine's grain exports.
Second- and third-generation biofuels use feedstocks that do not directly compete with food or feed crops, such as wastes and residues, to avoid the dilemma.
Second-generation fuels raise competition for lignocellulosic biomass and so its cost.
Responsible policies and economic instruments are needed to make biofuel production sustainable.

related: Indirect land use change from biofuels
contested_note: Sources flag the food-versus-fuel question as contested.

title: Indirect land use change from biofuels
article: Indirect land use change impacts of biofuels

definition.text: The unintended extra carbon emissions from land-use change elsewhere, caused by cropland expanding to meet global demand for biofuels.

facts.text: Farmers worldwide respond to higher crop prices by clearing pristine land to replace the food crops diverted to biofuel; because rainforests and grasslands store carbon, clearing them raises net greenhouse gas emissions.
Some authors argue it also affects biodiversity, water quality, food prices and supply, land tenure, worker migration and community stability.
Before 2008, life-cycle studies found corn, cellulosic and Brazilian sugarcane ethanol cut emissions versus gasoline, but none counted indirect land use change.

A 2008 Searchinger paper concluded that indirect effects offset the direct gains of corn and cellulosic ethanol; payback was 4 years for Brazilian sugarcane, 167 for US corn and 52 for cellulosic ethanol, over a 30-year horizon.
Critics such as Wang and Haq called the assumptions outdated, and Searchinger replied that ignoring these emissions is wrong however hard they are to predict; the studies stayed controversial.
In 2009 the California Air Resources Board included indirect land use change in the California Low-Carbon Fuel Standard, in force in 2011.
A 2010 Brazil study projected indirect deforestation of 121,970 km2 by 2020 from sugarcane ethanol and soybean biodiesel, a carbon debt taking about 250 years to repay.

contested_note: The size of indirect land use change emissions was disputed by the studies' authors and critics.

definition.text: A legal designation under the US Endangered Species Act of areas essential to conserving a listed species, even if the species does not occupy them yet.

facts.text: Designation does not bar development: it affects only federal agency actions, such as federally funded activities or those needing a federal permit, and creates no preserve or refuge.
Under Section 7 of the ESA, federal agencies must ensure their actions do not jeopardize a listed species or destroy or adversely modify its critical habitat.
Before designating, agencies must weigh economic and national security impacts; an area may be excluded if exclusion benefits outweigh designation benefits, unless exclusion would cause extinction.
Designation needs detailed population and ecological data, and good designations require compromise between environmental protection and economic needs.

definition.text: The rapid spread of cities and towns, often with low-density housing, single-use zoning and heavy reliance on the private car.

facts.text: Researchers admit the term lacks precision; it is the unrestricted spread of housing, commerce and roads over large areas with little concern for dense urban planning.
Single-use development separates homes, work, shops and recreation so far that walking, transit and cycling are impractical and every activity needs a car.
Sprawl often takes fertile farmland next to cities, and in the US a like-kind exchange tax break means the tax code subsidizes it.
Environmental effects include land consumption, habitat loss, lower biodiversity and local ecosystem destruction; a review found urbanization endangers more US species than any other human activity.
Sprawl raises driving, vehicle emissions and air pollution, cuts physical activity, and raises crash risk through greater exposure to driving.
Public services cost more in spread-out areas: roads, pipes, sewers and power lines are longer per household, so maintenance costs more.
Lost habitat and fragmentation raise contact between wildlife and people, which can raise vector-borne and zoonotic disease risk.

title: Urban sprawl debate

definition.text: The argument over whether sprawl is a market-efficient settlement pattern or a problem that planning should regulate.

facts.text: Critics argue sprawl creates more problems than it solves and should be regulated; proponents argue markets produce the most economically efficient settlements, and some market-oriented commentators see sprawl as the result of free-market distortions.
Whether sprawl reflects consumer preference is contested: Peter Gordon argues most households have shown a clear preference for low-density living.

Some critics worry anti-sprawl policy raises housing prices; evidence on Oregon is mixed, with one study showing the largest affordability loss and another showing Portland's rises similar to other Western cities.
Many critics concede sprawl creates negative externalities but dispute the best remedy; Gordon and Richardson argue new transit costs outweigh its benefits and land-use limits raise housing costs.

contested_note: Sources call the cause, costs and remedies of sprawl contested.

title: Smart growth
article: Urban sprawl#Alternative development styles > Contemporary anti-sprawl initiatives

definition.text: A planning approach that favors mixed-use, closely spaced development over sprawl.

facts.text: The term is used mainly in North America; "compact city" and "urban intensification" describe similar ideas in Europe, especially the UK, where they have shaped policy.
The American Planning Association and Smart Growth America favor mixed-use development with buildings near one another, to cut car use.
Maryland's 1997 Smart Growth Areas Act directed funding to areas already growing or with development plans.
Melia et al. (2011) found that raising population density does reduce car use, but weakly: doubling density will not halve how often or how far people drive.
